newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gold meltdown bad news for South African exports.
newsitem.headline: Gold meltdown bad news for South African exports.

text.p: Gold's New Year meltdown could deliver a fresh blow to South Africa's economy, hurting a hoped-for export recovery in 1997, threatening job losses in mines and hitting reserves, economists said on Wednesday.
But the fallout will be less than in the past, reflecting the declining role of gold in the economy of a country which is still the world's largest producer.

A weaker rand, cushioning mines from the full impact of the dollar price fall, should also help South Africa ride out current price weakness, analysts said. But a decline to $330 an ounce would spell serious trouble.
Gold was fixed in London at $355.80 per ounce on Wednesday against $359.00 on Tuesday.
The fixing was just above the lowest since October 6, 1993 when it was $353.50. Gold is down 3-1/4 percent since the start of this year when a steady slide started to accelerate.

In the last 10 years, gold's contribution to South Africa's total export earnings has virtually halved from 42.5 percent in 1986. But at 23.1 percent in 1995, according to the government's Minerals Bureau, it remains a significant source of hard currency.

"In terms of total export earnings it is not killing yet but if you talk about the price falling to $330 then it really would become a meaningful inhibiting factor," said Standard Bank chief economist Nico Czypionka.

"If gold does settle at lower levels, that impacts on the viability of marginal mines and mining houses will try and cut back, preserve cashflows and rationalise the labour force. That could have ramifications for whole towns."

Herman van Papendrop, economist at SMK Securities, agreed that the balance of payments would feel the pinch with potentially disappointing performance by gold offsetting an expected upturn in non-gold exports.
"Obviously any fall in the dollar gold price is going to be reflected negatively on the balance of payments, but much of that will be offset by the depreciation in the rand," he said.

However, gold's fall will have little if any impact on overall economic growth or on the government budget, since tax on gold mines contributes less than one percent of government income, analysts added.

The mining industry as a whole contributed only 7.7 percent to gross domestic product in 1995, down from 15.4 percent in 1986, and gold's share of that was less than half. Most economists are already expecting a slowdown in growth to around two percent in 1997 from an estimated three percent in 1996.

But the gold fall will take its toll on already low official reserves, currently equal to just four weeks import cover, especially since gold's share of total reserves has increased sharply from 34 percent at the end of 1995 to 54 in November.
Czypionka said the impact would be seen in January reserves.
The Chamber of Mines calculates that this month's fall in the gold price has increased the number of marginal mines among its 23 members to nine from six.
Marginal mines are defined as those with a working profit to working revenue ratio of less than seven percent.
Roger Baxter, the senior economist at the chamber, said the price fall to date should not have any immediate impact on production with output likely to stabilise around 500 tonnes in 1997.
But that could change radically if the gold meltdown, being driven by selling from investment funds, continues.

"At the moment the mines are still making money overall. But if the dollar gold price goes down to $330, at these exchange rates, then a lot of mines will start losing money and that could be horrendous," said van Papendorp.
